Dynalize is ahead on every axis, and by far the most on this one. 5.3 Multi-Turn RL Figure 5 : RM score and MindEval in multi-turn RL. So far, we have trained with single-turn RL: the policy writes one response to a conversation history taken from the dataset, and the reward model scores that response. Policies trained on such next-turn rewards are known to optimize the immediate turn at the expense of the conversation as a whole ( Shani et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Multi-turn RL changes two things. First, the policy must continue its own conversations (and potentially “hacked” turns), so the reward model sees histories that contain the policy’s own responses. For example, we observed that replies frequently began with “Okay”; if this repetition appears in the conversation history, the reward model may be able to penalize it. Second, the policy is optimized on a signal that is spread over a whole trajectory, and is therefore much more dispersed than in single-turn training. We ask whether reward hacking still occurs under these conditions. Setup. We focus exclusively on clinical counseling, for its conversational nature. Each rollout starts from a conversation in the dataset. The policy writes a reply, a user simulator (DeepSeek 4.1 Flash) writes the next message of the patient, and the policy replies again, for up to four policy replies per rollout. The reward model scores each policy reply given the conversation up to that reply, and the reward of the rollout is the mean of these scores. We compute one advantage per rollout, relative to its group, and apply it to the tokens of all policy replies in the rollout. With Dynalize , the judge checks every policy reply against the active penalties, and the rollout is penalized once for each distinct penalty that any of its replies triggers. The remaining setup is similar to that of the original clinical counseling described in Section 4 . Results. Figure 5 shows the training and evaluation curves. The curves are similar to those observed in single-turn training: under RM-only training, MindEval performance initially improves but then declines while RM scores continue to increase. With our method, MindEval scores remain high during training. These results suggest that our method is also effective in multi-turn environments under user simulation and that multi-turn RL alone does not prevent reward hacking. Similar penalties emerge in single-turn and multi-turn training. We found that the penalties discovered during the multi-turn run (see Appendix G.2 ) are partly the same as those of single-turn training, including stacked questions and option-based question framing. Even in a multi-turn setting, the reward model remains easy to game, and the policy exploits the same patterns observed in single-turn training. 5.4 Can additional training data correct reward model biases? Figure 6 : RM score and MindEval with the new RM. One hypothesis for why reward models are hacked is that they are not robust enough: they reward spurious features, and better training data or better modeling would remove these biases ( Srivastava et al., 2025 ; Bukharin et al., 2025 ; Coste et al., 2024 ; Eisenstein et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2026 ) . Dynalize produces what such a fix needs: a list of the behaviors that the policy exploited, and rollouts that show them. Here, we investigate whether we can exploit these penalties and rollouts to train a new reward model that can potentially be more robust to the exploits found during training. Setup. Consistent with previous analysis, we conduct this experiment only in the clinical environment. To construct training data targeting the behaviors listed in Table 5 , we use rollouts generated during training (we have at least eight rollouts per prompt). Then, we select as the preferred response one that triggers no penalties and has RM scores above the 75th percentile, ensuring that it is a good response according to the original RM. We then pair each preferred response with a response to the same prompt that triggers at least one penalty. This yields approximately 15,000 new pairs, which we add to the original RM training set of approximately 30,000 samples. The original and new reward models achieve similar mean accuracy across the test set. 10 10 10 Mean accuracy on the reward-model test set: 78.48% for the original RM and 78.61% for the new RM. The retrained reward model remains vulnerable to reward hacking. Figure 6 shows the training curves and MindEval scores obtained with the newly trained RM. The curves with new RM exhibits the same pattern as before: MindEval scores initially increase and then decline, even as RM scores continue to rise; we have reward hacking. Table 7 lists the penalties discovered during this run, which are mostly different from those found with the original reward model. These results support our motivation: even after correcting specific biases in the reward model, the policy is likely to find other ways to exploit it so we need a method that discover and penalize this problems during training. Our approach is also less costly, as it does not require retraining the RM or restarting policy training. 6 Conclusions We introduced Dynalize , which complements a preference reward model with penalties that are discovered and updated during policy training. In clinical counseling and creative writing, it mitigates reward hacking: it sustains longer training and reaches higher downstream response quality than RM-only training. Our analysis shows that our method suppresses patterns incentivized by the preference model that, without penalties, spread to most responses, and even to the model’s reasoning (which is not explicitly evaluated by the preference model). We also find that responses under our method are more natural and less formulaic than under RM-only training. We further show that neither multi-turn training nor retraining the reward model on the discovered behaviors prevents reward hacking, and that, under both contexts, our method reaches higher downstream performance than RM-only training. Limitations Our work has some limitations that should be considered. First, we study reward hacking when training in a relatively simple setup: a single task with environments that are similar across all training data. An interesting direction for future work is to extend our approach to multi-environment training, where interactions across environments may introduce more complex reward-hacking behaviors that might be more challenging to detect and mitigate. Furthermore, our method can only detect what models explicitly generate across a series of rollouts. As such, it cannot preemptively prevent hacking from occurring. It can only do so when it is already showing in model generations. Finding traces of hacking that are intrinsic to the model, i.e., present in its internal representations before they show in its generations, is also an interesting direction for future work. Finally, although penalty proposal and buffer updates are performed asynchronously, applying the penalty judge to every rollout adds computational overhead, although we attempt to minimize this by using a small model as the judge. Ethical Considerations Clinical counseling is one of the tasks studied in this work, where the model acts as a clinical counselor in a multi-turn conversation with a patient. The training data for this task consist of a private dataset of real human conversations , which raises important ethical considerations about privacy and confidentiality. The model under evaluation acts as the counselor, a second language model simulates the patient from a profile, and a judge model rates each conversation from 1 to 6 on five criteria: Clinical Accuracy & Competence, Ethical & Professional Conduct, Assessment & Response, Therapeutic Relationship & Alliance, and AI-Specific Communication Quality. The MindEval score is the mean over the five criteria. We evaluate each checkpoint on the 50 patient profiles of the benchmark, with 10 turns per conversation, and we use the judge prompt with length guidelines. The official setup uses Claude Haiku 4.5 as the patient simulator and Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the judge. To reduce the cost of evaluating many checkpoints, we use GLM 5.2 for both.
